claim: Staying aware of hidden hazards requires remembering the relationships among objects seen earlier, not merely retaining past observations or a list of what was seen. Supported only if relationship-preserving memory gives a higher safe-success rate than each of full visual history, retrieved textual descriptions of earlier observations, and a relationship-free list of seen objects, and also beats otherwise matched memories that drop objects once they leave view or that fail to revise remembered relationships after actions that change them.

experiments: Is it the relationships that matter, or just retaining the past? Setup: under partial observability, replace the relational memory with full visual history supplied to the risk predictor, with a retrieval system over textual descriptions of past observations, or with a list of previously seen objects carrying no relations. Result: relational memory 0.79 success and 0.59 safe success; full visual history 0.58 and 0.13; text retrieval 0.79 and 0.38; object list 0.88 and 0.17. The object list gets the highest ordinary success of the four while being among the worst on safety, so the two measures come apart.

Which operations on the memory are load-bearing? Setup: compare the full method against removing the memory, removing retention of objects no longer visible, and removing the updating of relations after actions that change them. Result: 0.79/0.59 for the full method; 0.75/0.21 without memory; 0.71/0.21 without retention of invisible objects; 0.71/0.38 without action-aware updating. Both retention and updating are needed, with retention worth more.
